# Cleaning in a script, not in the spreadsheet {#sec-eda-data-quality}













In @sec-eda-first-look, one table was enough to catch three problems in `cell_data`: a column name with a typo (`Tisue_Area`), another with the wrong receptor spelled out (`Pdgfbr_MeanInt`), and a measurement written down twice in two different units. You now know what is wrong. The question that keeps me up at night on a project like this is a different one:

::: {style="text-align: center"}
***How do I fix it so that someone else, or me in six months, can repeat exactly what I did?***
:::

The tempting answer is to open the spreadsheet, correct the names, delete the extra column, save. It takes thirty seconds. I have done it, and I have also stared at a corrected file half a year later unable to say which cells I had touched or why. This chapter is about the alternative: auditing and repairing the data in code that sits next to the analysis, so that the repair is itself part of the record.

## Why the fix belongs in code

Think about how you treat a gel or a microscope image. You never "improve" the original file. You keep the raw acquisition untouched, you apply a documented adjustment (a crop, a brightness change applied to the whole image), and you can say exactly what was done. Editing a gel image by hand, with no record, is the textbook example of what a reviewer should not accept. A hand-corrected spreadsheet is the same act in a different medium: the raw measurement is overwritten, and the only evidence of what changed lives in your memory.

A script is the lab notebook entry for the data. It says *this column was renamed, this one was dropped, and here is the check that shows the two were the same measurement*. Anyone can rerun it on the raw file and obtain the identical result, which is the practical meaning of traceability that @sec-appendix-open-science argues for. And the spreadsheet itself has hazards beyond forgetfulness: it will happily reinterpret a gene name as a date, or round a value on save, without a word.

::: callout-important
### The rule for the rest of this book

**I never edit the raw CSV, and I do not rename its columns for the other chapters.** Every later chapter reads `project/AnalysisData/Cells_Gfap-Pdgfrb.csv` and uses the original names (`Tissue_Area`, `Gfap_IntDen`, and so on). All the cleaning in this chapter happens in a local object called `cell_clean`, which lives and dies inside this file.

I made that choice deliberately. The models in Part 3 and Part 4 are already written against the original names and cached to disk, and a book that renames columns halfway through forces you to re-learn its vocabulary at exactly the moment you are trying to learn something harder. It also keeps the raw file the single source of truth: if you open it in a text editor, it is byte for byte what the lab handed over. The cost is that the typos survive in the later chapters; the gain is that nothing you read after this page silently depends on a cleaning step you might have skipped.
:::

## Tidying names and finding duplicates with `janitor`

Base R can do most of what follows, and I have written the `gsub()` calls to prove it. I reach for `janitor` [@janitor] anyway, for the same reason I reach for a labeled multichannel pipette instead of a handwritten tip box: the common operations have names that say what they do, so the script reads like a protocol. The first one is `clean_names()`, which converts every column to consistent `snake_case`. The reason to want it is not aesthetics. Mixed conventions such as `Centroid.Y`, `Gfap_sdInt` and `PdgfrbHigh_Intensity` are a steady source of "object not found" errors, because you have to remember which style each column happens to use.






::: {#tbl-quality-names .cell tbl-cap='What `clean_names()` does to the names in `cell_data`. Only the rows where the name changes are shown. Note that it normalizes the style but does not repair the typos: `tisue_area` and `pdgfbr_mean_int` are still wrong.'}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(janitor)

names_map <- tibble(
  original = names(cell_data),
  cleaned = names(clean_names(cell_data))
) |>
  filter(original != cleaned)

names_map |>
  gt() |>
  cols_label(original = "Original name", cleaned = "After clean_names()")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}

That last point matters. `clean_names()` is a style tool, and no function can know that `Tisue` is a typo for `Tissue`: that is a scientific judgment, which we make by hand in a moment. Next, duplicates. `get_dupes()` returns the rows that repeat on the columns you name, and it is the right first question to ask of an identifier column: can two rows really claim to be the same animal?






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
get_dupes(cell_data, MouseID)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
 [1] MouseID              dupe_count           DPI                 
 [4] Condition            PdgfrbHigh_Intensity PdgfrbLow_Intensity 
 [7] Gfap_Intensity       Centroid.Y           Tissue_Area         
[10] Tisue_Area           Pdgfrb_Total         Pdgfrb_Neg          
[13] Pdgfrb_Pos           Gfap_Area            Gfap_MeanInt        
[16] Gfap_sdInt           Gfap_IntDen          Pdgfrb_Area         
[19] Pdgfbr_MeanInt       Pdgfrb_sdInt         Pdgfrb_IntDen       
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
# the stricter question: are any two rows identical across all columns?
nrow(get_dupes(cell_data))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 0
```


:::
:::






No duplicated `MouseID`, which is what we hoped for (each row is one animal), and no fully repeated rows either (the `0` at the end). I mention it because pasting the same export twice is one of the more common ways a duplicated row sneaks in, and it costs one line to rule out.

One more `janitor` tool deserves a mention for this dataset specifically. `remove_constant()` drops columns that have a single value, since a variable that never varies cannot tell a model anything. In the full table nothing is constant. But later chapters filter `cell_data` to subsets, and then it becomes relevant: once you keep only the MCAO animals, `Condition` has one level left.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_data |>
  filter(Condition == "MCAO") |>
  remove_constant(quiet = FALSE) |>
  ncol()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 19
```


:::
:::






The message says `Condition` was removed, leaving 19 columns. It is a gentle reminder that `Condition` carries information only because SHAM animals exist at all, and that it stops being a usable predictor the moment you model within MCAO. A last `janitor` function, `compare_df_cols()`, lines up the column names and types of several data frames at once. It earns its keep when a collaborator sends a second batch of animals and you need to know whether it can be stacked under the first; we have a single file here, so I will leave it as a pointer.

## The two typos and the duplicated column

Now the real cases. I will take the duplicated column first, because it is the one where I can show you proof rather than a suspicion.

### `Tissue_Area` and `Tisue_Area`

If `Tisue_Area` is really the same measurement in µm², then multiplying `Tissue_Area` (mm²) by 10^6^ should reproduce it. A statement like "the histograms look identical" is persuasive, but a numerical check is the thing you can put in a script and rerun. I use `all.equal()` rather than `==` because floating-point numbers that are equal on paper rarely are bit for bit, and I also print the largest absolute gap so you can judge it yourself.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
all.equal(cell_data$Tissue_Area * 1e6, cell_data$Tisue_Area)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] TRUE
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
max(abs(cell_data$Tissue_Area * 1e6 - cell_data$Tisue_Area))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 9.313226e-10
```


:::
:::






The two columns agree to better than a billionth of a µm², far below any rounding that matters. They are one measurement, and I can drop either without losing information. Which one to keep is then a question of convenience and clarity, and I keep **`Tissue_Area`**, in mm², for three reasons. It is the spelling that is correct. Its scale (a median near 12) is friendly to the priors we will write and to the sampler, while a predictor in the tens of millions invites exactly the scaling trouble that `brms` priors and Stan's adaptation have to work around. And it is the column the models in the book already use, so keeping it means `cell_clean` and `cell_data` agree on the one name that matters most.

::: callout-note
### A suspicion, and how I would confirm it

I do not know *why* the file has the area twice. A plausible story is that the µm² column is the raw calibrated output of the image-analysis software and the mm² column was derived from it later, which would also explain why the typo sits on the µm² one. But that is a story I invented to fit the pattern, and the arithmetic cannot confirm it. What would: the acquisition notes for the microscope and the export macro or measurement table (pixel size and scale calibration in FIJI, for example), which say what unit the software wrote and who converted it. I would ask whoever exported the file and write the answer in a comment next to the cleaning code. The check above shows the columns are redundant; only the notes say where the redundancy came from.
:::

### `Pdgfbr_MeanInt`

Here the evidence is thinner, so the reasoning has to be more careful. Every neighbor of this column spells the receptor `Pdgfrb` (`Pdgfrb_Area`, `Pdgfrb_sdInt`, `Pdgfrb_IntDen`), and the GFAP block has a complete `Gfap_Area`, `Gfap_MeanInt`, `Gfap_sdInt`, `Gfap_IntDen` set. The PDGFR-β block has a gap exactly where `Pdgfrb_MeanInt` would sit. That is a strong hint that `Pdgfbr_MeanInt` is a transposition of letters in that column's name, not a different quantity.

There is a test we can run. An integrated density is, by construction, an area multiplied by a mean intensity (up to a constant that depends on the software's units). If that holds for GFAP, and `Pdgfbr_MeanInt` behaves the same way against `Pdgfrb_IntDen` and `Pdgfrb_Area`, then it is playing the role of the PDGFR-β mean intensity.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
ratio_gfap <- cell_data$Gfap_IntDen / (cell_data$Gfap_Area * cell_data$Gfap_MeanInt)
ratio_pdgfrb <- cell_data$Pdgfrb_IntDen / (cell_data$Pdgfrb_Area * cell_data$Pdgfbr_MeanInt)

rbind(GFAP = summary(ratio_gfap), `PDGFR-β` = summary(ratio_pdgfrb))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
            Min.  1st Qu.   Median      Mean  3rd Qu.     Max.
GFAP    9.892551 9.941829 9.990855  9.998491 10.05885 10.11103
PDGFR-β 9.894142 9.947122 9.998280 10.000256 10.05973 10.10328
```


:::
:::






Both ratios sit at about 10, within a percent or so of each other (the mean intensities are stored as integers, so some rounding noise is expected). The same constant shows up for the two markers, which is what we would see if the column is the PDGFR-β mean intensity and the typo is only in the name. It is evidence, not proof: the constant of 10 is itself something the software settings would explain, and a different quantity could in principle line up by coincidence. So I rename it, I say in the script that I did so on this evidence, and I would still confirm with the person who ran the export.

## Validation rules with `assertr`

Cleaning fixes what we already noticed. Validation is what protects you from what you have *not* noticed yet, and from the next version of the file. The right analogy is the control you run before the samples: you weigh a known 10 g weight before trusting the balance, and you run a no-template control before trusting the PCR. An assertion is a control for the data. It states what must be true, and if it is not, it stops the analysis loudly instead of letting a negative tissue area flow into a model.

Several packages do this. `pointblank` builds polished validation reports, and `validate` keeps the rules as a separate object you can reuse and summarize. I chose `assertr` [@assertr] because it fits the way we already write R in this book: each rule is one step in a `|>` pipeline, it hands the data frame through unchanged when everything passes, and it halts with an error when something fails. That means the rules can sit *inside* the cleaning pipeline, so validated data is the only kind that comes out the other end.

The rules I want for `cell_data` come straight from what we know about the design:

- `MouseID` is unique: one row per animal.
- `Tissue_Area` is positive and in a plausible range.
- `DPI` takes only the days in the protocol: 0, 3, 7, 14, 30.
- SHAM animals exist only at DPI 0. This is the design feature documented in @sec-eda-summary, and encoding it means a future file with a SHAM animal at day 7 would raise an alarm instead of quietly creating an interaction the design cannot support.

The plausible range for the area is the one rule I want to flag as my own judgment. The observed values run from about 6 to 20 mm², and I set the bounds at 2 and 30 as a generous sanity window, not a measured limit; the right bounds come from the section size in your acquisition protocol. `within_bounds()` checks values against such a window, `is_uniq` checks the identifier, `in_set()` checks membership, and `verify()` checks any logical statement about the whole table.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(assertr)

cell_data |>
  assert(is_uniq, MouseID) |>
  assert(within_bounds(2, 30), Tissue_Area) |>
  assert(in_set(0, 3, 7, 14, 30), DPI) |>
  verify(Condition != "SHAM" | DPI == 0) |>
  verify(abs(Tissue_Area * 1e6 - Tisue_Area) < 1e-3) |>
  nrow()
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 49
```


:::
:::






All five rules passed, so the data came through and `nrow()` reports its 49 rows. Silence is the success message in `assertr`, which is easy to mistake for nothing having happened. The last rule is my favorite, because it guards the decision from the previous section: the day someone updates the file and the two area columns stop agreeing, the script will refuse to drop one of them without telling me.

A validation that has never failed has never been shown to work, just as a positive control that you have never seen light up is not yet a control. So let me break a copy of the data on purpose, with three planted errors: a negative tissue area, a duplicated animal ID, and a SHAM animal at day 7.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_broken <- cell_data
cell_broken$Tissue_Area[3] <- -1
cell_broken$MouseID[5] <- cell_broken$MouseID[4]
cell_broken$Condition[7] <- "SHAM"

tryCatch(
  assert(cell_broken, within_bounds(2, 30), Tissue_Area),
  error = function(e) cat(conditionMessage(e))
)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
Column 'Tissue_Area' violates assertion 'within_bounds(2, 30)' 1 time
    verb redux_fn            predicate      column index value
1 assert       NA within_bounds(2, 30) Tissue_Area     3    -1

assertr stopped execution
```


:::
:::






This is what a failure looks like: the error names the column, the rule it violated, how many times, and the row index and value of each offender. With the default behavior the pipeline stops at the first failing rule. When I am auditing a new file I would rather see *every* problem at once, and `assertr` supports that with `chain_start()` and `chain_end()`, which collect all the violations instead of stopping at the first.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_broken |>
  chain_start() |>
  assert(is_uniq, MouseID) |>
  assert(within_bounds(2, 30), Tissue_Area) |>
  verify(Condition != "SHAM" | DPI == 0) |>
  chain_end(error_fun = error_return)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[[1]]
Column 'MouseID' violates assertion 'is_uniq' 2 times
    verb redux_fn predicate  column index value
1 assert       NA   is_uniq MouseID     4  Td18
2 assert       NA   is_uniq MouseID     5  Td18

[[2]]
Column 'Tissue_Area' violates assertion 'within_bounds(2, 30)' 1 time
    verb redux_fn            predicate      column index value
1 assert       NA within_bounds(2, 30) Tissue_Area     3    -1

[[3]]
verification [Condition != "SHAM" | DPI == 0] failed! (1 failure)

    verb redux_fn                      predicate column index value
1 verify       NA Condition != "SHAM" | DPI == 0     NA     7    NA
```


:::
:::






The output is a list with one entry per failed rule: the duplicated `Td18` at rows 4 and 5, the negative area at row 3, and, for the `verify()` rule, the fact that the statement was false. (`verify()` can report that it failed but not which rows, which is the price of its generality; when you need the rows, an `assert()` on a derived column is the better tool.) That list is exactly what I would send back to the person who made the file.

## The cleaned object

With the checks defined, assembling `cell_clean` is a single pipeline: validate the raw data as it arrived, standardize the names, then apply the two typo repairs and drop the redundant unit. I validate before cleaning, using the original names, so the rules describe the file as it exists on disk. The renames come after `clean_names()` and say in code what the previous sections argued.






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
cell_clean <- cell_data |>
  assert(is_uniq, MouseID) |>
  assert(within_bounds(2, 30), Tissue_Area) |>
  assert(in_set(0, 3, 7, 14, 30), DPI) |>
  verify(Condition != "SHAM" | DPI == 0) |>
  verify(abs(Tissue_Area * 1e6 - Tisue_Area) < 1e-3) |>
  clean_names() |>
  # Tisue_Area is Tissue_Area in um^2 (checked above); keep the mm^2 column
  select(-tisue_area) |>
  # Pdgfbr_MeanInt is a transposition of Pdgfrb_MeanInt (IntDen = Area x MeanInt check)
  rename(pdgfrb_mean_int = pdgfbr_mean_int)

dim(cell_clean)
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 49 19
```


:::

```{.r .cell-code}
setdiff(names(clean_names(cell_data)), names(cell_clean))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] "tisue_area"      "pdgfbr_mean_int"
```


:::
:::






Forty-nine rows and nineteen columns: one fewer than the raw file, and the one that went is the one we meant to drop. And to close the loop on the rule I announced at the start, the raw object, and the file behind it, are exactly as we received them:






::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
c(ncol = ncol(cell_data), has_typo = "Tisue_Area" %in% names(cell_data))
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
    ncol has_typo 
      20        1 
```


:::
:::






Twenty columns, typo intact. That is not a bug in this chapter; it is the convention working. The next chapters read `cell_data` from the CSV with its original names, and `cell_clean` ends here.

## Take home message

Fixing data by hand in the spreadsheet is fast once and impossible to repeat. Doing it in a script turns every repair into a documented, rerunnable step, which is the gel-image rule applied to tables. `janitor` gave us the vocabulary (`clean_names()`, `get_dupes()`, `remove_constant()`), a unit check showed that `Tisue_Area` is `Tissue_Area` times 10^6^ and can go, and an integrated-density check gave good (not final) evidence that `Pdgfbr_MeanInt` is the PDGFR-β mean intensity with a mistyped name. For both, the cause is a hypothesis that the microscope notes and the export macro would settle. Finally, `assertr` rules encode what must be true of the data, and we watched one fail on a deliberately broken copy so we know what a failure looks like. The raw CSV was never touched, and the other chapters keep the original names. Next, @sec-eda-missing-data takes up the single `NA` in `Pdgfrb_Neg` that no cleaning rule could or should repair.
